title: The Dragon and the Youngest Prince
subtitle: Animal helpers join the fight

dragon.work: Fairy Tales From Far and Near
dragon.author: Katherine Pyle
dragon.locator: Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals; Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals, normalized characters 12957-14901
dragon.excerpt: The Prince hid himself behind a heap of rocks and lay there watching, and presently he heard a great noise. It was made by a procession of people who were bringing the Princess down to the seashore. She was very beautiful, but so sad looking that the Prince’s heart melted within him for pity of her. They brought her to the seashore and left her there, and every one went away except two nobles of the Court. One of them was driving the coach that brought the Princess, and the other one sat beside him as footman. They were to wait until all was over, and then they were to take the news back to the King, but they kept the coach high up on top of the cliff where they would be out of danger. The Prince waited until all the others had left her, and then he came out from behind the rocks and went to speak to the Princess; but when she saw him she was frightened, for she did not know who he was nor whence he came. “Do not fear me,” the Prince said to her. “I mean you no harm, but instead I have come hither to do battle with the dragon, and if it may be, to save you.” When the Princess heard this, she begged and implored him to leave her. “Why should you perish also? None can ever do battle with yonder monster and come out alive.” But the Prince would not listen to her. And now the dragon bestirred itself and turned and came slowly toward the shore, and as it came they could smell the smoke of its breathing. The Prince drew his sword and stood waiting for it. Then as it came still nearer, the fox sprang out on a rock, dipped his tail in the salty water and slashed it across the eyes of the monster so that it was almost blinded. The lion and the bear also splashed up the water; the boar ripped at the dragon with his sharp tusks; the hare sprang upon its head and struck with its paws; and the Prince drew his sword and plunged it into the monster’s heart, so that the life blood ran out from it into the sea, and it was dead.
dragon.note: Verbatim text from Katherine Pyle's 1922 English children's retelling. The collection labels it Lithuanian but does not identify an oral informant or underlying source text.

narrativeBlocks.title: A princess is offered as a reward
narrativeBlocks.body: The youngest prince hears that a dragon threatens the country and that the king promises his daughter's hand to whoever defeats it.

narrativeBlocks.title: The prince delivers the final blow
narrativeBlocks.body: The fox splashes water into the dragon's eyes, the bear and boar attack, and the hare strikes its head; the prince's sword kills it.

narrativeBlocks.title: Keep the plot and source attribution distinct
narrativeBlocks.body: Pyle's story calls this a Lithuanian tale, but does not identify an informant or source-language text. Teach the episode as Pyle's retelling.

narrativeBlocks.title: Victory is collaborative
narrativeBlocks.body: The scene gives the animals active roles in the fight rather than making the prince succeed alone.
